Recovers the user terminal telemetry rows that your client missed while it was offline. The response is a link to a Parquet file. One row for each reading a terminal reported in the window.

### 1. The smallest request that works

Only `startDate` and `endDate` are required:

```json
{
  "startDate": "2026-09-07T08:00:00Z",
  "endDate":   "2026-09-07T10:30:00Z"
}
```

This gives you every device the tenant owns.

> **Read the example body below as a list of every field the endpoint accepts, not as the body you must send.** Send only the fields you need. The example shows `deviceId`, `deviceIds` and `vesselId` together, but you must never send them together.

### 2. Ask for less than the whole tenant (optional)

Add **one** of these to the body:

| To backfill | Add to the body |
| --- | --- |
| One device | `"deviceId": "0100…"` |
| Several devices | `"deviceIds": ["0100…", "0100…"]` — up to 500 |
| One vessel | `"vesselId": "0197…"` |

`deviceIds` and `vesselId` cannot go together. A request that has both answers `400`.

Leave all three out to get every device you own.

### 3. Rules for the time window

| Rule | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Format | RFC3339, UTC, for example `2026-09-07T08:00:00Z` |
| Longest window | 3 hours (`endDate` − `startDate`) |
| How recent `endDate` may be | at least 5 minutes in the past |
| Oldest `startDate` | 90 days |

`endDate` must be in the past so that the window is closed. A closed window gives a stable file.

### 4. What comes back

**`200` — the file is ready.**

```json
{
  "status": "ready",
  "downloadUrl": "https://slash-telemetry-backfill.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/…",
  "expiresAt": "2026-09-07T13:30:00Z",
  "rowCount": 35283,
  "sizeBytes": 1399945
}
```

Download `downloadUrl` directly. It is a presigned link and it needs no API key. It stops working at `expiresAt`, which is approximately 3 hours.

**`202` — the file is large, and the server is building it.**

```json
{ "status": "building", "retryAfter": 10 }
```

Send the **same** request again after `retryAfter` seconds. There is no separate status endpoint: the same request answers `200` when the file is ready. Repeating the request is cheap and does not count against your hourly limit.

**`404`** — you own no rows for that scope and that window.

**`429`** — too many requests. Wait and send the request again.

### 5. Points to remember

- The same request always gives the same file. Send it again to get a new link for a file you already have.
- The column names in the file are the same as the field names of `GET /telemetry/user-terminals`, so the code that reads that endpoint also reads this file.
- `includeAlerts` is not supported. A request with `includeAlerts: true` answers `400`. Use the `alerts-user-terminals` and `alerts-routers` endpoints instead.

get.description:
Returns one point per calendar day. By default the series is SPARSE — only days that carried a usage snapshot appear — so `totalCount` is the number of days WITH DATA in the window, not the number of days in the window. Set `fillEmptyDays=true` to get every calendar day: days with no snapshot come back with `totalGB` 0, `overageGB` 0, the previous day's `cumulativeGB` carried forward, the plan fields (`planKind`, `isUnlimited`, `entitlementGB`, `remainingGB`) carried forward, no `lastUpdatedAt`, and `synthesized: true` so filled days are always distinguishable from real ones. Days before the first real point of the window are filled with zeros and no plan fields. Filling happens BEFORE paging, so `page`, `limit` and `totalCount` then all describe the filled series and `totalCount` becomes the window length in days.
`dayBoundary` selects the calendar the days are cut on. `utc` (default) buckets on UTC. `site` buckets on the vessel's `oneweb_sites.timezone`: both which day a snapshot belongs to AND the window's leading edge move — the start instant is rounded down to the site-local midnight of the day it falls in, so the first day of the series is a whole local day; the end instant is unchanged, so the last day stays partial as it already is when `endDate` defaults to now. `timeRange` still echoes the requested instants. A site with no recorded timezone, or one the server's tzdata cannot load, falls back to UTC days with a WARN rather than failing the request.

get.description: Returns the terminal's state TRANSITIONS in the window, newest first, plus a window-start SEED per terminal. The seed is that terminal's latest transition strictly BEFORE "from", appended at the end of the array (it is the oldest entry) and flagged "seed": true. It exists because this table records transitions, not states: without it a terminal that stayed offline (or online) across the whole window returned an empty array, indistinguishable from a terminal that has never reported. A seed row is REAL — its stateChangeTime is its own true historical transition time, which is therefore outside the window; the flag says the transition predates the window, not that the row was invented. A terminal with no transition at all before the window gets no seed. Seeds are fetched independently of "limit", so a busy window can never evict them, and the response may hold up to limit (per terminal) plus one seed per terminal.

get.description:
Answers "how is the fleet doing this week" in one request. Buckets the 5-minute rows of `oneweb_perf_link_availability_v2` across every vessel the tenant owns and returns the fleet average, the five worst vessels, and a daily trend. It is `/oneweb/vessels/{vesselId}/connectivity/history` asked of the whole fleet, and it inherits that endpoint's window contract exactly: `from`/`to` RFC3339, **default the last 7 days**, **cap 90 days**, `400` beyond it.
SCOPE. Vessels are resolved through the usual vessel → site → `place_id` chain with the same non-empty `site_id` guard the terminal inventory carries, so a vessel saved with a blank site matches nothing rather than joining every place-less availability row in the table. `vesselCount` counts every vessel in scope; `vesselsWithData` counts the subset that produced at least one reading, and is the population the averages actually describe. Where a site backs several vessels, the fleet totals count it ONCE (both vessels genuinely share those terminals) while the ranking still lists both.
AVERAGES ARE SAMPLE-WEIGHTED. Each vessel's `avgAvailabilityPct` is a plain average over its own 5-minute readings, and the fleet's is a plain average over every reading from every distinct site — so a vessel with more readings pulls the fleet number harder, and a vessel observed for six hours is not comparable to one observed for six days on the average alone. `sampleCount` (288 per terminal per complete day) is what makes them comparable and is returned at both levels for that reason. `worstVessels` ranks only vessels WITH data: a vessel that reported nothing is unobserved, not bad.
NO ZERO-FILL, ANYWHERE. A day with no readings is absent from `trend` rather than plotted at 0%, and a fleet with no readings at all returns `avgAvailabilityPct: null` — never 0, which would assert the fleet was fully down. An empty fleet, or one with no data in the window, is a **200** with zero counts, a null average and empty arrays; there is no 404 on this route, because "you own no vessels" is an answer, not a missing resource. `trend` is TIME-ASCENDING, oldest first — the order a chart is drawn in, unlike the per-vessel history's newest-first points.
CAVEAT ON ZEROS (audit finding 7), and it applies to every number here: `availability_percent` is a plain `Float64`, so a STORED zero is itself ambiguous between a genuine outage and a missing reading — 15.5% of prod rows over 30 days are zeros (15.9% of dev's) — and that ambiguity propagates into the fleet average, the trend and the worst-vessel ranking alike. Until the column is made `Nullable`, read every percentage alongside its `sampleCount`.

get.description:
Answers "what is the fleet burning this cycle, and who is burning it" in one request. Every number comes from the SAME store internals the per-vessel and bulk usage endpoints use — the ranked atomic-snapshot read, the live-cycle overage scoping, the pool resolution — so a vessel's `totalGB` here is byte-identical to what `/oneweb/vessels/{vesselId}/data-usage/current` reports for it.
POOL AWARENESS is the part Starlink's equivalent never had to model. A OneWeb fleet is typically a set of POOLED SUB-PLANS whose own entitlement is `null` by design, because the quota lives on a parent POOL-* product; a rollup without it produces a total with nothing to compare it against. `pools` is always present and is the authority — one entry per distinct pool the fleet's active products name, each with the pool's own `entitlementGB` / `remainingGB` / `usedGB` and the `memberCount` of fleet products drawing on it. `pool` is a convenience alias for the single-pool case, and is OMITTED the moment a second pool appears rather than silently naming one of two — so read `pools` if you want code that survives that day. A pool the sub-plans name but the platform has never ingested rows for is still listed, with all three figures and `asOf` null: it is a real state (dev is in it today) and zeros there would describe an exhausted pool.
COUNTING. `vesselCount` is the tenant's ACTIVE vessels; inactive ones are excluded because they contribute nothing and would make the fleet look idler than it is. `activeServiceCount` counts DISTINCT ACTIVE SITE-CONNECTIVITY PRODUCTS — that is, LIVE TERMINAL SERVICES, not vessels with service. A site connectivity product is one terminal's service and a site can carry one per terminal, so a two-terminal vessel contributes 2. It therefore differs from `vesselCount` whenever a service is suspended, cancelled or absent (fewer), whenever two vessels share one site (the shared products count once), and whenever a vessel has more than one terminal in service (more). `totalGB` and `totalOverageGB` are summed over those same DISTINCT products: two vessels on one site share its counters and adding them twice would inflate the fleet by a whole vessel, while a multi-terminal vessel contributes each of its products once — OneWeb's counters are strictly per-product, so summing them never double-counts.
RANKING. `topConsumers` is descending by `totalGB`, at most `top` entries (default 10, max 100), over vessels with an ACTIVE product only — a vessel whose service is suspended has no current-cycle consumption to rank. Ties break on vessel name then id, so a fleet of idle vessels does not reshuffle between two identical requests. A vessel with an active product but no usage rows yet appears with zeros and an empty `planKind` rather than being dropped. A vessel whose site carries several active products is ranked on the SUM across them, which is the same number its own `/oneweb/vessels/{vesselId}/data-usage/current` reports; its `planKind` is empty when those products' kinds disagree (a standard plan beside a pooled sub-plan), because the vessel then has no single plan kind — the per-vessel endpoint's `products[]` carries the breakdown.
An empty fleet is a **200** with zero counts, empty `pools` and an empty `topConsumers` — there is no 404 on this route. Figures are labelled GB and passed through unconverted; a snapshot arriving in another unit is logged, never silently relabelled (prod and dev are 100% GB today).

get.description:
Per-terminal tracks over `[from, to)`, down-sampled IN CLICKHOUSE so a month of history costs the same to draw as an hour of it. The window is cut into `maxPoints` equal time slots per terminal and each slot collapses to ONE stored fix — the last one inside it. Points are therefore real observed positions with their real timestamps: nothing is averaged (which would put a vessel rounding a headland on dry land) and nothing is snapped to a slot boundary. Slots containing no fix produce no point, so a gap in the feed stays a gap in the track rather than being bridged.
`points` are TIME-ASCENDING, oldest first — the order a polyline is drawn in, and the one OneWeb series that is not newest-first. A terminal with no fix in the window is absent from `terminals`; a vessel with no track at all is absent from `vessels`, so `totalCount` counts vessels that actually moved into view.
HISTORY BEFORE 2026-08-22 IS THINNED. Until the `2026-08-22_ut_location_rekey` migration, `oneweb_perf_ut_location` was keyed `(primary_imei, measurement_start_time)` under ReplacingMergeTree, so several distinct samples sharing one start timestamp collapsed to whichever the merge kept — leaving roughly one surviving fix per sync interval. The lost rows are not recoverable. A pre-rekey window will therefore often return far fewer than `maxPoints` points per terminal, and that is the data, not the down-sampler.
BULK SEMANTICS, as on the current-location bulk route: unknown, malformed, hidden, soft-deleted and other tenants' ids are absent from the response rather than producing a 404.

The OneWeb Service Event feed — planned / emergency / expedited maintenance, incidents, and weather forecasts OneWeb expects to affect the network. This is a customer-visible differentiator: the Starlink API publishes nothing equivalent. Served from ClickHouse (`oneweb_service_events`, refreshed by the ingester), collapsed with FINAL to the newest generation of each event (every field but the id is mutable upstream — status flips inProgress→closed, dates get re-forecast).
ACCOUNT-LEVEL, NOT TENANT-SCOPED. The feed is shared distribution-partner reference data, returned IN FULL to every authenticated tenant, exactly like the product-offering catalogue — the tenant API key is the only gate. There is deliberately no per-tenant or per-vessel scoping because none is computable: an event names administrative REGIONS (`affectedRegions`, administrativeRegion codes — the join key to `oneweb_administrative_regions_v2`), not sites; a vessel carries no region and is mobile; and the regions table has no geometry to place a vessel in a region. A caller that wants regional relevance filters by `regionId`. `global: true` marks an event that names no regions and therefore affects the whole network.
ORDERING is `expectedStartDate` DESC then `id`, with events that have no start date grouped LAST (they have no schedule position); the id tiebreak keeps a page walk stable.

active.description: True when the alert was last sampled within ~2 minutes of now (still ongoing)

firstSeen.description: Earliest sample of this alert within the requested window

lastSeen.description: Latest sample of this alert within the requested window

sampleCount.description: Number of raw ~3.7s samples collapsed into this episode

models.RouterAlertResponse.description: Paginated response for router alert episodes

models.RouterTelemetry.description: Telemetry data from a Starlink router

models.RouterTelemetryResponse.description: Paginated response for router telemetry data

endDate.description: Scheduled or actual deactivation date as reported by Starlink. May be in the future for scheduled non-renewals, and may not coincide with the `active` flag flipping. Treat as advisory rather than an authoritative deactivation timestamp.

models.ServicePlan.description: Current service plan for a vessel: exactly one plan row (the latest applicable) joined with the current billing cycle. Fields not exposed by the upstream data are null instead of fabricated defaults.

allocatedDataGB.description: Data allocated to this service line for the current billing cycle, including proration when the plan started mid-cycle: a 500 GB monthly allowance activated on the 18th reports about 216.67. Null when the upstream publishes no per-line allocation blocks for the cycle (read blockDataGB instead, which reports the same current-cycle entitlement from a different upstream feed with broader coverage), and for plans with no per-line allocation such as pooled plans billed per GB from an account-level pool

autoRenew.description: Null when renewal behaviour is not available from the upstream data

blockDataGB.description: Data-block entitlement for the current billing cycle, from the service line's block feed. Like allocatedDataGB it is pro-rated for a partial cycle; where both are present they agree to within rounding. The two are kept separate rather than coalesced because they come from different upstream endpoints with different coverage, so a consumer can tell which source produced the figure

currentActivationDate.description: When the plan currently in force took effect. If the plan changed during the life of the service line, this is the most recent change rather than the line's original start date

firstActivationDate.description: Earliest subscription start recorded for this service line. Scoped to the service line rather than the terminal, so a terminal moved onto a new line reports that line's first activation

isOptedIntoOverage.description: Whether the service line is opted into overage billing

overageDescription.description: Description of the overage product attached to the plan; omitted when none

overageName.description: Name of the overage product attached to the plan; omitted when none

price.description: Null when the plan price is not available from the upstream data

standardDataGB.description: Null when the upstream data does not expose a standard-data allowance for the plan

subscriptionEndDate.description: Set when the subscription has a scheduled end; omitted for open-ended plans

topUpDataGB.description: Overage and one-time purchase data for the current billing cycle. Reported separately from allocatedDataGB because a top-up is purchased once the plan allowance is exhausted, so it is not part of what the plan itself allocates

models.ServicePlanHistoryPoint.description: One point per billing cycle: the freshest cycle snapshot joined with the plan that was applicable when the cycle started. Fields not exposed by the upstream data are null instead of fabricated defaults.

autoRenew.description: Null when renewal behaviour is not available from the upstream data

isOptedIntoOverage.description: Whether the service line was opted into overage billing

overageDescription.description: Description of the overage product attached to the plan; omitted when none

overageName.description: Name of the overage product attached to the plan; omitted when none

price.description: Null when the plan price is not available from the upstream data

standardDataGB.description: Null when the upstream data does not expose a standard-data allowance for the plan

subscriptionEndDate.description: Set when the subscription has a scheduled end; omitted for open-ended plans

active.description: True when the alert was last sampled within ~2 minutes of now (still ongoing)

firstSeen.description: Earliest sample of this alert within the requested window

lastSeen.description: Latest sample of this alert within the requested window

sampleCount.description: Number of raw ~3.7s samples collapsed into this episode

timestamp.description: Deprecated alias of lastSeen, kept for backwards compatibility

models.UserTerminalAlertResponse.description: Paginated response for user terminal alert episodes; totalCount is the number of alert EPISODES in the window (not raw samples)

models.UserTerminalTelemetry.description: Telemetry data from a Starlink user terminal (dish)

ipAllocation.description: BETA: present only when the request was made with `includeIps=true` and an IP poll exists in the row's minute bucket. Omitted otherwise. The embedded shape may change without notice based on user feedback.

models.UserTerminalTelemetryResponse.description: Paginated response for user terminal telemetry data

serviceLineNickname.description: User-defined nickname for the vessel's service line. Empty string when no nickname is set.

serviceLineActive.description: Whether the vessel's service line is active. Defaults to false if service line not found.

serviceLineAddressReferenceId.description: Identifier of the address associated with the vessel's service line. Multiple vessels at the same physical address share this value.

serviceLineProductReferenceId.description: Identifier of the Starlink product (plan) associated with the vessel's service line.

publicIpEnabled.description: Whether the vessel's service line has a public IP assigned.

lastUpdatedAt.description: Timestamp of when the data was last ingested (RFC 3339 format), null if no data available

nonBillableGB.description: Diagnostic or non-billable data consumed by this vessel.

optInPriorityGB.description: Portion of priority data consumed while opted in to overage. Already included in priorityGB — not added on top of it.

priorityGB.description: Total priority data consumed by this vessel (includes all unrestricted data, including any opt-in overage usage).

standardGB.description: Standard (deprioritized) data consumed by this vessel.

totalGB.description: Sum of priorityGB + standardGB + nonBillableGB. optInPriorityGB is NOT added separately since it is already part of priorityGB.

models.VesselLatestTelemetry.description: Latest telemetry and alert data for a Starlink vessel. stale=true when the device has not reported within the requested window; lastSeenAt is null when it has been silent beyond the 7-day retention of the latest-telemetry view.

lastSeenAt.description: Last telemetry sample ever recorded for this device; null when it has been silent beyond the 7-day retention of the latest-telemetry view

latestRouterAlertTimestamp.description: Latest Router Alert (nullable if no alerts)

latestTerminalAlertTimestamp.description: Latest User Terminal Alert (nullable if no alerts)

stale.description: True when the device has not reported telemetry within the requested timeRangeHours window

models.VesselLatestTelemetryResponse.description: Paginated response for vessel latest telemetry and alert data

locationCount.description: Number of location points for this vessel

models.VesselPatchRequest.description: Request body for patching vessel details. All fields are optional — only non-null fields will be updated. account_number cannot be changed.

service_line_number.description: Service line number associated with the vessel
Service line number to assign to the vessel. Must exist under the tenant's permitted account and not be assigned to another vessel.

vessel_serial_number.description: Optional vessel identifier (IMO number, MMSI, call sign, etc.)

status.description: Optional vessel status. Defaults to 'active' if not provided.

granularity.description:
Granularity declares the OUTPUT resolution the series was computed at,
and is present ONLY when that resolution differs from what the rows are
stored at — today that means exactly `granularity=1 hour`, where every
sample is a query-time aggregate over 5-minute rows rather than a row.

It is omitted on the raw path (`granularity` empty or "5 minutes") for
two reasons: each raw sample already carries its own stored
`granularity`, so the envelope would add nothing; and omitting it keeps
the raw response byte-for-byte what it has always been, which is the
guarantee that made repurposing the parameter safe to ship.

activeProductId.description:
ActiveProductID is the PRIMARY active site-connectivity product — the
most recently updated one, id ascending on a tie. ProductIDs is the
AUTHORITY: a site connectivity product is a single terminal's service,
not "the vessel's plan", and a site can carry one per terminal, so this
field names one of possibly several. It is retained for wire
compatibility with clients written before that was understood.

productIds.description:
ProductIDs are all the ACTIVE site-connectivity products at the vessel's
site, most-recently-updated first. The product-keyed series (throughput)
query every one of them; the IMEI-keyed series use Terminals, which is
the union of these products' terminals.

asOf.description:
AsOf is DATA time, not response time: the newest measurement timestamp
among the samples actually returned below. It is nil (omitted) when no
metric returned a sample.

BEHAVIOUR CHANGE (2026-08-24): this used to be time.Now() at response
assembly, which made an offline vessel look freshly measured — a
day-old snapshot carried a second-old asOf. Consumers that treated it
as "when the server answered" must switch to the HTTP Date header;
consumers that treated it as data freshness (its documented meaning)
now finally get the truth. A vessel that has stopped reporting now has
an asOf that visibly ages, and no asOf at all once its last sample
falls out of the 24h lookback.

degraded.description:
Degraded lists, by JSON field name, the metrics whose query FAILED for
this request. Those fields are omitted from the response and the
snapshot is still returned with 200 — one sick table no longer costs
the caller every other metric. Absence from this list is the guarantee:
a metric that is omitted and NOT named here simply had no sample in the
lookback window. Omitted entirely when nothing failed; if every metric
fails the request is a 500 instead, because an all-degraded 200 would
be an empty snapshot dressed up as a successful one.

products.description:
Products is the per-product breakdown the scalars above aggregate.
Always present (never null); one element per ACTIVE site-connectivity
product at the vessel's site, ordered newest-updated first.

seed.description:
Seed marks a sample that predates the requested window: the terminal's
LATEST transition strictly before `from`, prepended so the series says
what state the terminal was already in when the window opened. Without
it, a terminal that stayed offline (or online) across the entire window
produced zero rows — indistinguishable from "this terminal has no data
at all".

The row is REAL, not synthetic: stateChangeTime is its own true
historical transition time, which is therefore outside the window.
`seed: true` says exactly that — "this transition predates the window
and is carried in as the standing state" — and never "this value was
invented". Absent (false) on every in-window transition.

counterReset.description:
CounterReset is true when at least one counter on this sample was lower
than on the previous one. The affected counters report their current
raw value; counters that rose normally still report an honest diff.

bucketStart.description:
BucketStart is the bucket's left edge in UTC (toStartOfHour /
toStartOfDay of measurement_start_time). The bucket covers
[bucketStart, bucketStart + bucket width).

sampleCount.description:
SampleCount is the exact number of 5-minute readings folded into the
bucket — 12 for a complete hour, 288 for a complete day. Anything less
means the feed had gaps inside the bucket, so it is the honesty control
on the three percentages above: an average over 3 readings is not an
average over 288, and only this field says which one you got.

bucket.description:
Bucket echoes the resolved bucket width, "hour" or "day", so a caller
who omitted the parameter still knows what it got.

terminals.description:
Terminals holds one series per terminal that has at least one bucket in
the window. A terminal with no readings at all is omitted entirely —
consistent with omitting empty buckets, and distinguishable from "0%
available all week" for the same reason.

Terminals is one entry per terminal in Context.Terminals, in that order,
so a terminal the platform knows about but has no state for is still
listed (with State "unknown") rather than silently missing. When the
vessel context resolved no terminals at all, this instead lists whatever
terminals the site's transition history contains, IMEI-ordered.

vesselState.description:
VesselState is the ANY-ONLINE aggregate over Terminals: "online" if at
least one terminal is online, else "offline" if at least one terminal's
state is known and none is online, else "unknown".

Why any-online rather than all-online: a vessel's terminals are
redundant paths to the same ship, so one live path means the ship is
reachable — which is the question this endpoint exists to answer. The
per-terminal detail is right there in Terminals for a caller who needs
to know that a second UT is down.

"unknown" is reserved for genuine absence of evidence — no terminals
resolved for the vessel, or none of them has ever transitioned — and is
never used to mean "some terminals are unknown". A vessel with one
online and one unknown terminal is online.

bucketStart.description:
BucketStart is the UTC start of the day (toStartOfDay of
measurement_start_time); the bucket covers [bucketStart, +24h).

sampleCount.description:
SampleCount is the number of 5-minute readings from across the whole
fleet that the day's average is built from.

trend.description:
Trend is TIME-ASCENDING, oldest first — the order a line chart is drawn
in, and the same call the location tracks make. It differs from the
per-vessel connectivity history's newest-first ordering deliberately:
there, newest-first exists so the per-terminal safety cap truncates the
oldest buckets; here nothing truncates (90 days of daily buckets is 91
points), so the only consideration left is the plotting order.

Days with no readings are ABSENT rather than zero-filled, exactly as in
the per-vessel history. Never nil.

window.description:
Window echoes the resolved [from, to), so a caller that omitted both
still knows which seven days it got.

avgAvailabilityPct.description:
AvgAvailabilityPct is the average over ALL readings from all the
tenant's distinct sites — sample-weighted by construction, so a vessel
with more readings pulls it harder than one with a handful. It is NULL,
not 0, when the window produced no readings at all: a zero here would
assert the fleet was 0% available, which is the same fabrication the
per-vessel history refuses when it omits empty buckets.

sampleCount.description: SampleCount is every 5-minute reading folded into AvgAvailabilityPct.

terminalCount.description:
TerminalCount is the number of DISTINCT terminals that reported in the
window, counted over distinct sites so a site backing two vessels
contributes its terminals once.

vesselCount.description:
VesselCount is every vessel IN SCOPE — the tenant's visible,
non-deleted vessels that carry a site id — whether or not any readings
exist for them. It is the denominator the other counts are read against.

vesselsWithData.description:
VesselsWithData is the subset that produced at least one reading in the
window, and therefore the population AvgAvailabilityPct actually
describes. When it is smaller than VesselCount the fleet average says
nothing whatsoever about the difference — those vessels were not
observed, which is not the same as having been unavailable.

worstVessels.description:
WorstVessels is the bottom-5 ranking by AvgAvailabilityPct, ascending
(worst first), over vessels WITH DATA only. A vessel that reported
nothing is not "bad", it is unobserved, and ranking it last would be a
confident wrong answer. Never nil — an empty array when nothing
reported.

pool.description:
Pool is a convenience alias for Pools[0], present ONLY when the fleet
draws on exactly one pool — which is every real fleet today.

The two fields exist together on purpose. A single-pool response can be
read either way, so a client written against `pool` keeps working; the
day a tenant acquires a second pool, `pool` disappears rather than
silently naming one of two, and `pools` — which that client should have
been reading — still answers correctly. Omitting `pool` is a visible
change at exactly the moment a hidden one would have been wrong.

pools.description:
Pools is the AUTHORITY on pooled quota and is always present (an empty
array for a fleet with no pooled service). One entry per distinct parent
pool the fleet's active products name.

topConsumers.description:
TopConsumers is descending by TotalGB, at most `top` entries, over
vessels with an ACTIVE product only. Never nil.

totalGB.description:
TotalGB / TotalOverageGB are summed over DISTINCT active products, not
over vessels. Two vessels bound to one site share those products and
their counters; adding them twice would inflate the fleet total by a
whole vessel's consumption. A multi-terminal vessel contributes each of
its products once — the counters are strictly per-product, so summing
them never double-counts.

vesselCount.description:
VesselCount is every ACTIVE vessel in scope, including those with no
live service.

ActiveServiceCount counts DISTINCT ACTIVE SITE-CONNECTIVITY PRODUCTS —
live terminal services — NOT vessels with service. A site connectivity
product is a single terminal's service, and a site can carry one per
terminal, so a two-terminal vessel contributes 2. The two counts
therefore differ whenever a vessel's service is suspended, cancelled or
missing (fewer services than vessels), whenever two vessels share a site
(the shared products are counted once), and whenever a vessel has more
than one terminal in service (more services than vessels).

totalCount.description: TotalCount is len(Vessels): vessels with at least one track.

window.description:
Window echoes the resolved [from, to), so a caller that omitted both
still knows which 24 hours it got.

totalCount.description:
TotalCount is len(Vessels) — the number of vessels in THIS response, not
the tenant's fleet size. These endpoints are unpaged (a fleet's worth of
coordinates is a few KB), so the two numbers coincide except when
`includeVesselsWithoutFix` is false, where the count is deliberately the
plottable fleet.

vessels.description:
Vessels are ordered by (vesselName, vesselId). The id is the tiebreaker
that makes the order TOTAL: vessel names are not unique, so without it
two identically-named vessels would swap places between two identical
requests.

asOf.description:
AsOf is the snapshot's effective_date. Non-nil exactly when a pool
snapshot was found, so it is also the unambiguous signal for the
all-null case above.

entitlementGB.description:
EntitlementGB / RemainingGB / UsedGB come from the pool product's own
latest cycle snapshot, read with the identical ranked, atomic-snapshot
query the per-vessel usage endpoints use.

ALL THREE ARE NULL TOGETHER when the pool has no ingested rows at all —
the pool is named (the sub-plans say so) but the platform has never seen
its counters. That is a real state, not an error: dev holds exactly it
today, and reporting zeros would claim an exhausted pool. When a
snapshot IS present, AsOf is set, UsedGB is the pool's own reported
cumulative, and Entitlement/Remaining are individually null only if the
pool row itself carries no quota.

memberCount.description:
MemberCount is how many of the fleet's DISTINCT active products draw on
this pool. It is a count of products, not vessels: two vessels sharing
one site share one product and count once.

poolId.description:
PoolID is the POOL-* product id the fleet's sub-plans name as their
parent.

planKind.description:
PlanKind is the usage snapshot's plan kind ("sub_plan", "standalone",
…), empty when the product has an active binding but no usage rows yet —
and also empty when the vessel's site carries several active products
whose kinds DISAGREE (a standard plan beside a pooled sub-plan, which
prod does have). One vessel then has no single plan kind, and naming one
of two would be a guess; the per-vessel data-usage endpoint's products[]
carries the breakdown.

serviceState.description:
ServiceState is the winning site-connectivity product's own status.
Every vessel listed here has an ACTIVE one — that is the entry
condition — so this is always "active" today; it is carried anyway so
the field means the same thing it does on every other usage payload.

totalGB.description:
TotalGB is the vessel's CURRENT-CYCLE cumulative and OverageGB the
overage attributed to that same cycle — the identical numbers
/oneweb/vessels/{vesselId}/data-usage/current reports, because they come
from the identical store internals.

On a site carrying more than one active site-connectivity product (one
per terminal) these are the SUM across those products. OneWeb's usage
counters are strictly per-product, so summing never double-counts.

avgAvailabilityPct.description:
AvgAvailabilityPct is a PLAIN average over every 5-minute reading this
vessel's site produced in the window — each reading weighs the same, so
a vessel observed for six hours and one observed for six days are not
comparable on this number alone. SampleCount is what makes them
comparable, which is why it is here and not optional.

sampleCount.description:
SampleCount is the exact number of 5-minute readings behind the average
— 288 per terminal per complete day. The same honesty control the
per-vessel connectivity history carries per bucket, for the same reason:
an average over 12 readings is not an average over 2016.

measuredAt.description:
MeasuredAt is the real `measurement_start_time` of a real stored fix —
the LAST one inside its slot. Nothing here is interpolated or snapped to
a slot boundary, so consecutive points are not evenly spaced when the
feed had gaps, and that unevenness is the truth about the data.

points.description:
Points are NEWEST FIRST, matching every other OneWeb series. That is
also the functionally correct order for the per-terminal safety cap: the
cap truncates the tail, so it drops the oldest buckets rather than the
ones the caller almost certainly wanted.

lastSeen.description:
LastSeen is OneWeb's own last-contact timestamp for the terminal, read
from the Resource Inventory feed (`oneweb_user_terminals_v2
.last_seen_date`) — the same value `/oneweb/user-terminals` reports
under this name. It is an INDEPENDENT signal from Since, on a different
table and a different refresh cadence, so the two routinely disagree
(dev 2026-08-24: terminal 353565860047906 last transitioned 08-11 but
was last seen 08-03). Omitted when the inventory holds no row for the
terminal, or holds a zero timestamp (dev: 16 of 493 rows).

since.description:
Since is the time of that transition: the instant the terminal entered
the state it is still standing in. It is the endpoint's freshness signal
and no other is offered: a transition three weeks old speaks for itself,
and inventing a "stale after N hours" threshold would replace a fact the
caller can judge with a guess the api-layer cannot justify. Omitted
exactly when State is "unknown".

state.description:
State is the resource_state carried by this terminal's most recent
transition — "online" | "offline" — or "unknown" when the transition
table holds no row for it at all.

siteId.description:
SiteID is the vessel's OneWeb `LOC-*` place — the join key the fixes were
found through, included so a caller debugging a missing vessel can see
which site was searched.

terminals.description:
Terminals holds one entry per terminal WITH a fix, IMEI-ordered. It is
empty only for a vessel returned under `includeVesselsWithoutFix=true`;
by default such vessels are absent from the response entirely, because
the consumer is a map and a vessel with no coordinates has nothing to
draw. Never nil — an empty array, so JSON consumers can iterate blindly.

measuredAt.description:
MeasuredAt is `measurement_start_time` of the winning row: when the fix
was taken, not when it was ingested or served.

It is THE freshness signal, and the only one. There is no staleness flag
and no server-side default cutoff — same rule as the connectivity
endpoint's `since`: a three-week-old position speaks for itself, and a
threshold the api-layer invented would be a guess dressed as a fact. A
caller that wants a bound asks for one with `maxAgeHours`, and then a
terminal whose newest fix is older than the bound is reported as having
no fix at all rather than being quietly aged.

terminals.description:
Terminals holds one track per terminal that has at least one fix in the
window. A terminal with none is absent rather than carrying an empty
array, and a vessel with no moving terminal at all is absent from
`vessels` — same no-zero-fill rule as the connectivity history.

points.description:
Points are TIME-ASCENDING, oldest first — the order a track is drawn in.
This is the one OneWeb series that is not newest-first, and deliberately:
the per-vessel /performance/location series is a sample list where the
newest row is the interesting one, while this is a polyline.

imei.description:
IMEI is also the terminal's addressing identifier. OneWeb stores it as
user_terminal_id; the dedicated imei column is a sparsely-populated
duplicate that never disagrees with it, so this is resolved from
user_terminal_id when the column is empty.

resourceState.description: Live device state from the user-terminal inventory.

siteConnectivity.description: SiteConnectivity is this terminal's own service.

userTerminalId.description:
UserTerminalID is what the OneWeb write APIs address a terminal by — the
value to pass as ut_id when rebooting, muting or upgrading it.

affectedRegions.description:
AffectedRegions are the administrative regions the event names, zipped from
the table's parallel affected_location_{ids,names,types} arrays. Empty for
a global event.

expectedStartDate.description:
ExpectedStartDate / ExpectedEndDate are upstream-optional (Nullable in the
table); either is omitted when OneWeb has not forecast it.

global.description:
Global is true when the event names no affected regions: it affects the
whole network, so AffectedRegions is empty.

activeProducts.description:
ActiveProducts is the id/name/planKind/status summary of the site's active
products (len == ActiveServiceCount). Not the full allowance/bandwidth/IP
shape — that is the site-connectivity product endpoint's job.

activeServiceCount.description:
ActiveServiceCount is the number of active site-connectivity products at the
place; TerminalCount is the number of user terminals bolted to it. Both are
LIGHT counts, not the #432 per-service/per-terminal expansion.

endCustomer.description:
EndCustomer is reference detail (see the type doc). Omitted when every field
is empty.

installationHeight.description:
InstallationHeight is the user-terminal installation height. Omitted when
the amount is zero and the units are empty — the table default for a site
OneWeb never reported one for.

primaryContact.description:
PrimaryContact / AlternativeContact are reference-only party detail, omitted
when empty. Never used for authorization (see the type doc).

terminals.description:
Terminals is the id + resource_state summary of the terminals at the site
(len == TerminalCount). Not the full inventory shape — that is the
user-terminal endpoint's job.

vessels.description:
Vessels are the tenant's vessel(s) at this site — usually exactly one. It is
what makes the site visible to the tenant at all (the scoping chain), so it
is always present and non-empty on a returned site.

reportState.description:
ReportState is the state of the performance report this row was extracted
from (only "completed" reports are ingested). Omitted when empty.

utManufacturer.description:
Hardware provenance carried on every row by the ingester so sensor
analytics can filter/aggregate by UT family without a second lookup.
Omitted when empty; a model the ingester could not classify carries the
literal "Unknown" (not empty), which is itself informative.
